title: Heat turns female frogs into males, and the population could collapse within decades
dek: In a matter of days during a heat wave, female agile frogs develop testes and become reproductively capable males — but their offspring are also more prone to sex reversal, the compensation mechanism fails, and models predict population collapse within decades.
why: Both stories point to the unexpected consequences of climate change. The frog segment has a complete mechanistic chain and model predictions; the tick segment is closer to a news roundup.
who: Researchers studying the ecological impacts of climate change, people working on species conservation and population modeling, and readers who want to understand how sex reversal mechanisms propagate into population collapse.
skip: The 9:23–10:23 autumn book recommendations, unrelated to this episode's topic.

points.h: A few days of heat is enough to make female frogs grow testes
points.body: Agile frogs use the same XX/XY sex determination system as humans: XX is female, XY is male. But Veronica Bocconi says that simply exposing genetically female individuals to a few days of heat wave causes them to develop testes and become "apparently completely normal males." In fish and amphibians, heat turning individuals into males (female-to-male) is a fairly typical pattern, while most turtles are the exact opposite. This means that under the same climate warming, the sex ratios of these two groups of animals will move in completely opposite directions.

points.h: Sex reversal was originally a stop-loss strategy for a bad childhood
points.body: Why would letting temperature determine sex be advantageous? Bocconi's explanation is that this mechanism is useful when offspring may land in wildly different environments and some of those environments are especially unfavorable to one sex. If an agile frog encounters a heat wave in childhood, its development and growth are both slowed, making it hard to reach the body size and age needed to enter the adult population — it may not even survive long enough to reproduce. But if it switches to a male phenotype, it can start reproducing earlier, because males typically begin reproducing at a smaller body size. This is driven by "sex-dependent fitness effects." The question is whether that benefit still holds once the environment becomes more extreme.

points.h: Plastic buckets as honeymoon suites, experiments at the pond's edge
points.body: Sex reversal has been studied very little in the wild. Bocconi's approach exploits the fact that the frogs' breeding season is highly concentrated — for about three weeks each year they gather together, so she doesn't have to chase them around like colleagues studying Australian desert lizards. She sets up "sex hotels" by the breeding pond: a row of plastic buckets, one room per pair of frogs. She pairs a sex-reversed male and a sex-concordant male each with a female, and observes whether the female accepts them, whether she produces fertile eggs and offspring, and how the tadpoles fare afterward. This semi-natural setup is the foundation of the entire experimental chain.

points.h: Sex-reversed males can reproduce, but they only produce daughters
points.body: Although XX males have chromosomes that don't match their phenotype, they still possess the full equipment needed for reproduction and are fertile males. But when an XX male is paired with an XX female, the offspring are all XX at the genetic level — meaning in theory they should all be female. The trouble is that these offspring themselves undergo sex reversal — experiments show that the offspring of sex-reversed fathers are more likely to undergo sex reversal. Bocconi describes it as a positive feedback loop: warming turns more females into males, and sex-reversed males could compensate by producing XX offspring, but those offspring reverse into males too, so the compensation falls through and the sex ratio only skews further toward males.

points.h: Female frogs use reduced egg-laying to pick their mates
points.body: By measures of fertility, offspring survival rate, and the number of eggs a female lays, sex-reversed males are entirely normal. The only anomalous signal comes from "cryptic female choice": a female frog can't stop a male from clasping her, but if she doesn't like him, she can lay only a small portion of her eggs, letting the male think she's finished and release her, while she saves the rest for a future mate. Normally a female frog lays only one clutch per breeding season. The experiment was repeated over two years, and in both years some females did this split egg-laying with sex-reversed males, while they almost never did so with sex-concordant males. The sample size is small, but Bocconi believes "something may really be happening."

points.h: Heat wave plus virus, and the offspring of sex-reversed males can't take it
points.body: The researchers first subjected tadpoles to a heat wave, confirming that the offspring of sex-reversed fathers were more prone to sex reversal; they then continued rearing them and tracked mortality — that year was the hottest on record for that country, so an extra heat-related mortality study emerged by accident, but no difference in mortality was seen. Back in the lab, after infecting them with a ranovirus that is particularly vicious to these frogs, a difference appeared: if the father was a sex-reversed male and the tadpole had experienced heat treatment, these juveniles carried high viral loads. Bocconi's phrasing is "heat first, then virus, and they just can't take it."

points.h: Model prediction: this kind of species has only decades left
points.body: Feeding these data into the theoretical model they had developed earlier, and plugging in the known parameters for agile frogs, the model predicts that no matter what, as long as the climate keeps warming, this kind of species has only decades left before population collapse. If sex-reversed males cannot compensate for the skewed sex ratio — whether because females won't accept them, because their offspring all become male, or because the offspring die of the virus — then extinction will arrive sooner than that. Bocconi adds that what worries her more is ponds drying up completely, weather that could make the extinction scenario arrive even faster.

points.h: There is no universal conservation plan, only population-by-population calculations
points.body: Sea turtles are the ready-made example of this concern: people are already discussing how to control beach temperatures so that not all hatchlings come out male. But Bocconi stresses that temperature reaction norms vary greatly between species — not just in the direction of "heat produces males or heat produces females," but also in the critical absolute temperature at which the effect kicks in. So it's hard to give a universal strategy, but it is meaningful for a specific population: know the current water temperature of this pond or wetland network, predict what it will become, and then decide what kind of microhabitat to create so that offspring at least have a chance to choose an environment that produces males or females.
